extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy; attendees of William James's lectures (advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and educated public interested in metaphysics and philosophical method)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and comparing rival metaphysical or spiritual philosophies (monistic/absolutist vs pluralistic/radical empiricist) with emphasis on their epistemic, practical, and methodological virtues and defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intimacy versus foreignness (criterion of human participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the system make human beings intimate parts of the divine/world or treat them as outsiders and mere subjects? (Contrast: God as 'heart of our heart' vs God as 'magistrate' and truth 'instituted and established without our help'.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer views that allow human participation in truth and moral life (intimacy). Anti-pattern: doctrines that render our knowing or acting purely passive — e.g. scholastic theism where 'the most we can do is to acknowledge [truth] passively.' Consider how the view affects the felt relation between persons and the ultimate reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of lived history and temporality
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the philosophy respect time, history, and the categories of finite experience, or does it treat reality as 'timeless' and thereby de-realize ordinary life?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value philosophies that make 'the very life we lead seem real and earnest' (pluralism/timeful accounts). Anti-pattern: absolutist accounts that deny succession, suffering, surprise, or patience (the absolute 'can't be surprised... can't be guilty'), which risk alienating human sympathies. Assess whether the doctrine preserves human agents' capacity to act, suffer, and influence history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical/psychological consequences (trust vs wariness)
rubrics_metrics.description: How does the worldview shape practical attitudes — e.g., a background of intimacy tends toward trust, while a background of foreignness tends toward wariness and suspicion?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate philosophies by their pragmatic effects on conduct and social temperament. Example: materialism often produces distrust; spiritualistic intimacy produces more embracing, trusting dispositions. Consider what habits of life the system fosters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit with scientific and social advances
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the philosophy accommodate or remain compatible with contemporary scientific knowledge and social ideals (e.g., evolutionism, social democracy), or does it appear obsolete?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer conceptions that do not feel 'puerile' or out of keeping with advances in science and changing moral imagination. Anti-pattern: clinging to monarchical theism's juridical images when they no longer speak to the intellectual climate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of impressionistic argument — demand for technical rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious discussion requires technical, rigorous argumentation; 'impressionistic philosophizing' is 'intolerable to experts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test doctrines by analytic, technical critique rather than by rhetorical or emotional appeal. Example guidance: when a claim is presented as a 'logical necessity' it should be examined in detail rather than accepted on the basis of grandeur or authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward arguments that are purely verbal or semantic
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept 'reductio ad absurdum' arguments that rely merely on the abstract naming of properties rather than on concrete processes (e.g., Lotze's argument that distinct things cannot interact is treated as 'purely verbal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require explanatory depth: show the actual mechanism or concrete account of interaction rather than resolving the issue by renaming 'many' as 'one.' Anti-pattern: resolving conceptual difficulty by substituting one abstract name for another without supplying concrete content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'vicious intellectualism' (misuse of naming)
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not treat a name's abstract definition as excluding whatever the definition fails positively to include ('The treating of a name as excluding from the fact named what the name's definition fails positively to include, is what I call "vicious intellectualism"').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualify abstract predicates with concrete adjectives; do not let the bare word 'independent' or 'one' be used to deduce impossibilities. Practice: take predicates 'secundum quid' (in the specified respects) rather than 'simpliciter.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification of predicates (use of 'secundum quid')
rubrics_metrics.description: Always specify in what respects properties such as 'independence' or 'oneness' are meant; avoid unqualified absolutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct abstract consequences by restoring concreteness through qualifying adjectives. Example prescription: 'Don't take your "independence" simpliciter; take it secundum quid.' This prevents drawing false conclusions from overbroad abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation by experiential fit (each-form vs all-form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which metaphysical form better fits human experience — the 'all-form' (monistic absolute) or the 'each-form' (pluralistic/distributed reality)? The pluralistic 'each-form' is defended as offering higher intimacy and a more reasonable fit to our finite experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess metaphysical proposals by how well they accord with the mode of our experience: pluralism claims to preserve the concrete multiplicity and partial interrelations we live within, whereas monism may erase the temporality and participatory character of experience. Use experiential plausibility as a substantive criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resilience to authority-based influence (test coercive presuppositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that a metaphysical principle is a presupposition 'implicated in all thinking' must be tested by analysis, not conceded because of academic authority or rhetorical power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept a doctrine merely because of its institutional weight or eloquent proponents ('If weight of authority were all, the truth of absolutism would be thus decided'). Instead, expose and examine its argumentative structure and implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should keep doors open to neglected interests
rubrics_metrics.description: No philosophic system should aim to be so exclusive as to 'lock out any interest forever'; its proper ambition is to avoid permanently excluding other legitimate concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer systems that allow for multiple standpoints or leave room for other 'doors' of interest. Anti-pattern: designs that attempt to define nature so that 'no one's business is left out' (which James calls sure to fail). Value modesty and plural accommodation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory responsibility for interactions and relations
rubrics_metrics.description: When philosophers posit interaction between distinct entities they must explain how such interaction concretely occurs (what the process of influence consists in), not merely infer unity by claiming that an influence would otherwise be a third unexplained fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand concrete accounts of how influence or relation arises (James criticizes Lotze's and Royce's treatments and shows the need to specify the process rather than rely on semantic moves). Anti-pattern: invoking an 'immanent operation' or higher knower as a terminus without mechanistic or descriptive detail.
